title: the Lalita Sahasranama (selections)
hook: who wrote the names? the story inside the text: goddesses of speech, a crowded court, and a hymn handed to everyone

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama held two ways of speaking side by side: won over by devotion, and without form. What did you love that no picture could hold? A new week. Day one thousand one hundred seven.

The court is full. Gods, goddesses, sages, attendants, packed in before the throne of the goddess Lalita. Then a group of goddesses steps forward, the goddesses of speech, and they begin to recite. Name after name after name. That's the scene the Brahmanda Purana gives for where the Lalita Sahasranama came from. The whole hymn is set inside a conversation: Hayagriva, a horse-headed form of Vishnu, teaching the sage Agastya. And when Agastya hears the names, he's also told how they began. Today, the story of who wrote the names, and what the goddess did when she heard them.
screen: `A FULL COURT.` → `THE GODDESSES OF SPEECH.` → `WHO WROTE THE NAMES?`

segments.voice: Here's the story, in paraphrase, as the text tells it. Lalita calls the goddesses of speech, the Vagdevis, Vashini and her companions. She asks them to compose a hymn of her secret names, so that her devotees might have a way to please her. They compose it. Then, one day, with the whole court gathered, the goddess signals to them, and the Vagdevis stand and recite the names they've made. When they finish, the court is amazed. And the goddess, pleased, turns to everyone assembled and tells them to recite it: this hymn, made at her command, is the way to her favor. Two things in the story are worth a second look. First, the authors. In the story the names weren't put together by a poet at a desk. They came from the goddesses of speech themselves, and some readers take that as the reason the hymn is honored the way it is: speech itself, praising the one it comes from. Second, what happens to the hymn. It begins as something called secret, composed in a palace. And by the end of the scene, it's handed to a whole roomful of beings, with an instruction to use it. The story doesn't treat the names as a treasure to lock away. Tradition does keep some reverence around them; some teachers say the hymn should be received from a teacher, not picked up casually. Both of those live side by side. But the scene itself ends with the doors open. A hymn of praise, commissioned by the one being praised, and then given away.
screen: `LALITA CALLS THE GODDESSES OF SPEECH.` · `THEY COMPOSE HER SECRET NAMES.` · `THEY RECITE THEM IN THE FULL COURT.` · `SHE TELLS EVERYONE TO RECITE IT.` · then, large: `COMMISSIONED, THEN GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: one name, received. Settle, and let the breath slow. Choose one name from the hymn that you've met this past week: the one who gives grace, the one fond of devotion, the one without form. Or simply the name Lalita. Say it once, quietly, and then let it rest. Don't repeat it fast. Let the silence after it be as long as the name. Then say it again. If you pray, you can offer the name back to the goddess each time. If you don't, notice what a single word does when it's given room. The bell holds the time.
The Lalita Sahasranama. In the text's own story, composed by the goddesses of speech at Lalita's command, and given to everyone in her court. Today's word.

Your line: the Lalita Sahasranama, in selections. Today, pass on one good thing you were given, a recipe, a song, a piece of advice, the way the court was handed the names. Day one thousand one hundred seven.

howItsDone: Some devotees learn the Lalita Sahasranama from a teacher and recite it daily or on Fridays; in a temple or home archana, a name is offered with each flower or pinch of kumkum, in the form 'om … namah.'

sources.ref: Brahmanda Purana, Lalitopakhyana: the Lalita Sahasranama's frame (Hayagriva and Agastya; the Vagdevis compose and recite the names)

notes: The composition story is paraphrased from the frame chapters around the Sahasranama: Lalita commands Vashini and the other Vagdevis to compose a hymn of her secret names for her devotees; they recite it in her assembly; she is pleased and tells the assembly to recite it. Confirm the details and sequence, and whether 'the court is amazed' is in the text.
The number of Vagdevis (traditionally eight) is deliberately not spoken.
'Some teachers say the hymn should be received from a teacher' reflects the reverence around rahasya (secret) names; confirm fair.
'Some readers take that as the reason the hymn is honored': attributed, not stated as fact; confirm.
